implementation_notes: No language supports or provides the pattern — the poltergeist is an artefact of a design decision, and the remedy is to remove it. Detection is a lifetime question, which is language-neutral: find every construction of a type, and check whether the constructed value is ever stored, returned, or passed onwards. Construct-then-use-once-then-discard is the shape; a name containing Helper, Utils or Manager raises the prior. Before deleting, ask the three questions the practitioner discussion recommends: is there a more natural home for the method (the owning class, an extension on the target type, a function on the target type's module)? Is more than one caller using it? Does it need state — if it accumulates configuration, it is a builder and not a poltergeist. Then delete the class and put the call where the data lives, rather than inheriting the helper into the invoked class, which cements an unvalidated design.
idiom_name: transient object with no state; remedy is Move Method + delete
pitfalls: Judging on 'stateless and short-lived' alone catches valid builders and adapters.
Moving the method to the nearest plausible class instead of the one that owns the data.
Rescuing it by adding more one-line methods, which converts the poltergeist into a utility class.
